```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  # so return the already-filtered document unchanged.
  if (

      !any(grepl("<!-- SOLUTION START -->", lines, fixed = TRUE))
  ) {

  }

  if (solutions_only) {
    # Keep only the solution blocks, and promote their "**Solution N.**"

    keep <- rep(FALSE, length(lines))
    inside <- FALSE
    for (i in seq_along(lines)) {
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION START -->")) {
        inside <- TRUE
        next
      }
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION END -->")) {
        inside <- FALSE

      }
      if (inside) {
        lines[i] <- sub(
          "^\\*\\*Solution ([0-9].*?)\\.\\*\\*$",
          "## Solution \\1",
          lines[i]
        )
        keep[i] <- TRUE
      }
    }
  } else if (!show_solutions) {
    # Question-only version: drop the solution blocks.
    keep <- rep(TRUE, length(lines))
    inside <- FALSE
    for (i in seq_along(lines)) {
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION START -->")) {
        inside <- TRUE
        keep[i] <- FALSE
        next
      }
      if (identical(lines[i], "<!-- SOLUTION END -->")) {
        inside <- FALSE
        keep[i] <- FALSE
        next
      }
      if (inside) keep[i] <- FALSE
    }
  } else {
    # Questions and solutions together.
    keep <- rep(TRUE, length(lines))
  }

  paste(lines[keep], collapse = "\n")
})
```

This exercise follows **Chapters 8 and 13** of Collett, *Modelling Survival Data
in Medical Research* (4th ed.).
Questions 9–10 are optional extensions.

## Data and software

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sta310r)
library(survival)
library(broom)

options(digits = 3)

# Qualify data set names that are also used by survival.
bmt <- sta310r::bmt_leukaemia
ov <- sta310r::ovarian
rat_data <- sta310r::rats
```

## A time-dependent explanatory variable

In Collett's Example 8.2, patients are followed from bone marrow
transplantation until death or censoring. Platelet recovery means the
platelet count has returned to the level specified in `?bmt_leukaemia`.
We study whether the rate of death is associated with platelet recovery
status during follow-up.

**1.**

(a) Read `?bmt_leukaemia`. Identify the follow-up time, event indicator,
recovery time and disease group. How many patients died, and how many of
those died without a recorded platelet recovery?

(b) Inspect patients 7 and 8. What does the missing recovery time for
patient 7 mean? At the time of patient 7's death, would patient 8 be
classified as recovered?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 1.**

(a) Follow-up is `time` in days from transplantation, `status` is the
death indicator, `ptime` is the day of platelet recovery and `group` is
the leukaemia group.

```{r}
with(bmt, table(status, precovery))
```

There were `r sum(bmt$status == 1)` deaths, including
`r sum(bmt$status == 1 & bmt$precovery == 0)` without prior recovery.

(b)

```{r}
bmt |>
  filter(patient %in% c(7, 8)) |>
  select(patient, time, status, precovery, ptime)
```

Patient 7 died without reaching the specified platelet level. The missing
`ptime` reflects the absence of a recovery event. Patient 8 was alive at
day `r bmt$time[bmt$patient == 7]`, but recovered on day
`r bmt$ptime[bmt$patient == 8]`. Patient 8 was therefore still in the
unrecovered group at the time of patient 7's death.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**2.** Use `tmerge()` to create counting-process data with a death indicator
`death` and a time-dependent recovery indicator `recovered`. Use `event()`
to define the endpoint and `tdc()` to update recovery. Supply only patients
with a recorded recovery to the second call.

NOTE: `tmerge()` is in the `survival` package. See `?tmerge` for its
operational arguments, including `tdc()` and `event()`.

(a) Print the intervals for patients 7 and 8. Explain the interval
convention and where the death indicator is placed.

(b) Check that all interval lengths are positive and that expanding the
data preserves the numbers of patients and deaths.

(c) At patient 7's death time, how many patients in the risk set had already
recovered and how many had yet to recover? Use the interval endpoints to
select the risk set.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 2.**

(a)

```{r}
cp <- tmerge(bmt, bmt, id = patient, death = event(time, status))
cp <- tmerge(
  cp,
  filter(bmt, precovery == 1),
  id = patient,
  recovered = tdc(ptime)
)

cp |>
  filter(patient %in% c(7, 8)) |>
  select(patient, tstart, tstop, death, recovered)
```

Each row represents $(\mathrm{tstart},\mathrm{tstop}]$. Patient 7 contributes
one interval ending in death. Patient 8 contributes one interval before
recovery and another after recovery. Recovery changes the covariate for the
next interval. Only the interval ending in death has `death = 1`.

(b)

```{r}
c(
  patients = n_distinct(cp$patient) == nrow(bmt),
  deaths = sum(cp$death) == sum(bmt$status),
  positive_lengths = all(cp$tstart < cp$tstop)
)
```

(c)

```{r}
day <- bmt$time[bmt$patient == 7]

cp |>
  filter(tstart < day, day <= tstop) |>
  count(recovered)
```

The interval ending at `day` contributes to its risk set, including the
patient who dies then. A new interval starting exactly at `day` contributes
only afterwards.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**3.** Fit two Cox models for death, adjusting both for the three disease
groups with `factor(group)`.

(a) In the one-row-per-patient data, use `precovery` as if it were a baseline
explanatory variable. In the counting-process data, use current
`recovered` status. Report the recovery hazard ratio and 95% confidence
interval from each fit.

(b) Explain how the fixed analysis classifies patient 8 at the time of
patient 7's death. What bias can this introduce? Which association would
you report, and how would you describe the comparison?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 3.**

(a)

```{r}
fixed <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ precovery + factor(group), data = bmt)
updated <- coxph(
  Surv(tstart, tstop, death) ~ recovered + factor(group),
  data = cp
)

tidy(fixed, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "precovery")
tidy(updated, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "recovered")
```

(b) The fixed analysis counts patient 8 as recovered even before the
recovery day. Patients classified as ever recovered had to survive until
recovery. Assigning that earlier time to the recovered group can create
immortal time bias.

The time-dependent model compares the instantaneous death rates for
patients who have recovered and those who have yet to recover, at the
same time since transplantation and within the same disease group.
Its estimated hazard ratio is closer to 1 than the fixed estimate, and
its confidence interval includes 1.
Platelet recovery is a prognostic marker that can reflect underlying
health. The association alone gives no causal effect of inducing recovery.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## A time-dependent coefficient

`ovarian` contains follow-up from randomisation to death or censoring
(Collett, Example 8.3). Here age is recorded at baseline. We allow its
coefficient to vary with time since randomisation.

**4.**

(a) Define age in decades, centred at 60 years, and fit a Cox model with
this age variable and treatment. What does the age hazard ratio compare?

(b) Use `tt()` to add an interaction between age in decades and
$(t-365)/365$, where $t$ is follow-up time in days. Keep the main effects
of age (as derived from (a)) and treatment. Why is $t$ the current risk-set time? At what
follow-up time does the main age coefficient give the log hazard ratio
per decade?

NOTE: `tt()` is a special term in `coxph()`. See `?coxph` for its
documentation.

(c) From the model in (b): Calculate the age hazard ratio per decade at days 100 and 400.

(d) Compare the models from (a) and (b) by a likelihood ratio test with one degree of freedom.
Is there evidence that the age hazard ratio varies over time?

NOTE: `tt()` expands the risk sets internally, which prevents a direct
`anova()` comparison with the proportional hazards fit (you need some lower level calculations).

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 4.**

(a)

```{r}
ov <- ov |> mutate(age10 = (age - 60) / 10)

ph <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age10 + factor(treat), data = ov)
tidy(ph, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

The age hazard ratio compares women who differ by ten years of age at
randomisation, within the same treatment group. The proportional hazards
model uses the same ratio throughout follow-up.

(b)

```{r}
varying <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age10 + factor(treat) + tt(age10),
  data = ov,
  tt = \(x, t, ...) x * (t - 365) / 365
)
coef(varying)
```

All women in a given risk set are compared at the same event time. Using
each woman's eventual observed follow-up time as $t$ would use information
from after that risk-set comparison. At day 365 the interaction is zero,
so the main age coefficient gives the log hazard ratio per decade at
that time.

(c)

```{r}
days <- c(100, 400)
b <- coef(varying)
tibble(
  day = days,
  hr_per_decade = exp(
    b[["age10"]] +
      b[["tt(age10)"]] * (days - 365) / 365
  )
)
```
The fitted age hazard ratio becomes smaller later in follow-up.

(d)

```{r}
lr <- 2 * as.numeric(logLik(varying) - logLik(ph))
pchisq(lr, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

The likelihood ratio test gives little evidence for the added term, and
there are only `r sum(ov$status)` deaths. The point estimates alone do
not establish a change with time. The partial log likelihoods can be
compared directly because both models use the same patients and events.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## Recurrent events in the counting-process format

In Collett's Example 13.2, rats were randomised to retinoid prophylaxis or
control and followed for detection of mammary tumours. Several tumours
could be detected in the same rat. Read `?sta310r::rats` for the treatment codes and
how the recorded times handle multiple tumours found at the same visit.

**5.**

(a) Arrange the rows by rat and time. Within each rat, create a start
time and an event-order variable. Print the rows for rats 3 and 17.
Explain the difference between an interval's event order and the
`status` at its end.

(b) Check the number of rats, number of tumours and whether any intervals
have zero or negative length. Create a data set for time to first tumour.
How many tumour events does it contain, and what information is omitted?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 5.**

(a)

```{r}
rat_intervals <- rat_data |>
  arrange(rat, time) |>
  mutate(
    start = lag(time, default = 0),
    event_number = row_number(),
    .by = rat
  )

rat_intervals |> filter(rat %in% c(3, 17))
```

Each row uses time since randomisation, with the previous tumour time
(or zero) as its start. Event order indicates the tumour number the rat
is currently at risk of. On a censored interval, that next tumour was
not observed.

(b)

```{r}
rat_intervals |>
  summarise(
    rats = n_distinct(rat),
    tumours = sum(status),
    nonpositive = sum(start >= time)
  )

rat_first <- rat_intervals |> filter(event_number == 1)
sum(rat_first$status)
```

The first-tumour data retain one interval per rat. They describe when a
rat first develops a tumour and omit all subsequent tumour times.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## The Andersen–Gill and Prentice–Williams–Peterson models

**6.**

(a) Fit a Cox model for time to first tumour and an Andersen–Gill (AG) model
using all the intervals. Use `cluster = rat` in the AG fit. Report the
estimated treatment hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Explain
which events and risk sets each model uses.

(b) Refit the same AG model without clustering, using `robust = FALSE`.
Compare the estimated treatment coefficients and standard errors.
What does clustering by rat change, and why?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 6.**

(a)

```{r}
first <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment, data = rat_first)
ag <- coxph(
  Surv(start, time, status) ~ treatment,
  data = rat_intervals,
  cluster = rat
)

tidy(first, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
tidy(ag, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

The first model compares the rates of first tumour in the two groups
among rats still tumour-free and under follow-up. The AG model compares
the intensities of tumour detection among rats currently at risk,
regardless of their previous tumour count. It uses a common baseline
intensity across event orders.

(b)

```{r}
ag_model_based <- coxph(
  Surv(start, time, status) ~ treatment,
  data = rat_intervals,
  robust = FALSE
)
tibble(
  variance = c("Model-based", "Cluster-robust"),
  coefficient = c(coef(ag_model_based), coef(ag)),
  standard_error = c(sqrt(vcov(ag_model_based)[1, 1]), sqrt(vcov(ag)[1, 1]))
)
```

The estimated coefficients agree. The cluster-robust standard error in
these data is larger. The fit uses the same risk sets and partial
likelihood. The variance calculation allows contributions from the same
rat to be dependent, treating different rats as independent clusters.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**7.**

(a) On day 80 after randomisation, count how many rats are eligible for the
AG risk set and how many are eligible for the PWP risk set for a second
tumour. Explain the difference.

(b) Fit a Prentice–Williams–Peterson (PWP) model on time since randomisation.
Use a common treatment coefficient, stratify by event order and combine
the fifth and later orders as in the Chapter 13 exercises. Cluster by
rat. Compare the estimated treatment hazard ratio and interval with the
AG results. What is allowed to differ across the strata?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 7.**

(a)

```{r}
risk80 <- rat_intervals |> filter(start < 80, 80 <= time)
nrow(risk80)
risk80 |> filter(event_number == 2) |> nrow()
```

The AG risk set includes all rats under observation and at risk on day
80. For the PWP second-tumour comparison, a rat must already have had a
first tumour and still be at risk of its second at that time.

(b)

```{r}
rat_intervals <- rat_intervals |>
  mutate(event_stratum = pmin(event_number, 5))

pwp <- coxph(
  Surv(start, time, status) ~ treatment + strata(event_stratum),
  data = rat_intervals,
  cluster = rat
)
tidy(pwp, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

Both fits estimate a lower tumour intensity for the retinoid group.
The PWP estimate is closer to 1 and its confidence interval is narrower
in these data. The PWP comparison is made within event-order strata.
The first four orders
each have their own baseline intensity, and the fifth and later orders
share another baseline. The model fits one treatment hazard ratio
across these strata. A model with separate treatment coefficients by
event order would answer a different question.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**8.** A trial team records every hospital admission over two years.
The team wants both a comparison of the intensity of admissions
throughout follow-up and a comparison restricted to patients still at
risk of a second admission. Which models would you use? How would you
represent time spent in hospital if a patient cannot have another
admission until discharge? Explain how you would handle repeated records
from the same patient when reporting uncertainty.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 8.**

An AG model can address the first question by including all eligible
admissions. For the second question, fit a PWP total-time model restricted
to the second-admission stratum, or fit event-order-specific treatment
coefficients and report the one for the second admission. Both approaches
condition that comparison on a first admission. The clock can measure
time since trial entry for both analyses.

A patient who cannot be admitted again while already in hospital is out
of the risk set from admission to discharge. Use intervals that end at
admission and resume at discharge. A patient whose stay lasts until the
end of follow-up contributes no further at-risk time. Cluster standard
errors by patient to allow for dependence among records for the same
person.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

## Optional extensions

**9.** Restrict the rats data to the first four event orders and fit two PWP
models with the same event-order strata, one using *total time* and one
using *gap time*. Define time zero for the first and for later tumours in
the gap-time fit. Compare the treatment estimates and explain how the
time scale changes the comparison.

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 9.**

```{r}
first_four <- rat_intervals |>
  filter(event_number <= 4) |>
  mutate(gap = time - start)
pwp_total <- coxph(
  Surv(start, time, status) ~ treatment + strata(event_number),
  data = first_four,
  cluster = rat
)
pwp_gap <- coxph(
  Surv(gap, status) ~ treatment + strata(event_number),
  data = first_four,
  cluster = rat
)
tidy(pwp_total, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
tidy(pwp_gap, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

The gap clock starts at randomisation for the first tumour and restarts
after each tumour. A final censored interval contributes the time since
the last tumour until censoring if its event order is included. Both
fits use the same event orders, and the gap-time estimate is somewhat
further below 1 in these data. The gap-time fit compares rats at the
same elapsed time since the start of the current interval, within the
same stratum. The total-time fit compares rats at the same elapsed time
since randomisation.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->

**10.** Fit a shared gamma frailty model for recurrent tumours with a
frailty for each rat. Explain what is shared and interpret the treatment
hazard ratio. How does this approach differ from using cluster-robust
standard errors in the AG model?

<!-- SOLUTION START -->

**Solution 10.**

```{r}
shared <- coxph(
  Surv(start, time, status) ~ treatment + frailty(rat, distribution = "gamma"),
  data = rat_intervals
)
tidy(shared, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "treatment")
```

Each rat has an unobserved multiplicative factor shared by its tumour
intensities. The treatment hazard ratio compares rats with the same
frailty. This changes the intensity model to account explicitly for
between-rat heterogeneity. Clustering the AG standard errors groups
the variance contributions by rat without fitting a rat-specific
frailty.

<!-- SOLUTION END -->
